patterns.title: The Stag Hunt: Cooperation Under Uncertainty
patterns.domain: Strategic and game-theoretic problems; assurance, strategic uncertainty, and ranked coordination equilibria

sources.title: Rousseau, Discourse on Inequality (1755)
sources.supports: Historical deer-and-hare passage and participants leaving their posts for an individual opportunity.
sources.read_method: Original translated passage and its surrounding discussion read.
sources.boundary: Philosophical illustration, not a fully specified modern game or empirical account of actual prehistoric behavior. No numerical payoff or formal equilibrium result attributed to Rousseau.

sources.title: Skyrms, The Stag Hunt (2001)
sources.supports: Assurance-game structure, contrast with the prisoner’s dilemma, belief-dependent best responses, risk versus mutual benefit, variations of the safer action payoff, and risk dominance.
sources.read_method: Author-hosted March 2001 presidential address read, especially pages 1–4 and notes on assurance and risk dominance.
sources.boundary: A formal and philosophical account, not measured hunting returns or tutor utilities or evidence for the proposed guarantee. The hunters’ and tutors’ qualitative preference comparisons are original editorial assumptions, not utilities estimated by this source.

current_example_check.read: Reopened foundational text: stag/hare assumptions and conditional best responses, pp. 1–4.
current_example_check.boundary: Current teaching example is a qualitative editorial translation, not an observed intervention outcome.

sources.title: Charness, Self-Serving Cheap Talk: A Test of Aumann’s Conjecture (2000)
sources.supports: Written one-way pre-play messages in Stag Hunt variants, random-rematching methods, and sensitivity to whether the sender communicates before or after choosing an action.
sources.read_method: Published PDF methods, treatment payoffs, results, and interpretation read.
sources.boundary: The filename includes 2003, but the PDF is Games and Economic Behavior 33 (2000), 177–194. Sessions used ten periods of anonymous random rematching within six-person subgroups, not ten repeated encounters with one known partner. Communication results do not validate a guarantee or all promises.

patterns.short_description: Recognize when mutually beneficial cooperation depends on confidence in others, then distinguish building credible assurance from reducing the loss if cooperation fails.
use_when: Which choice is best when the other hunter joins?
goals: Recognize the familiar situation and preserve the defining mechanism.
Distinguish formal assumptions, empirical findings, and hypothetical continuations.
Make intervention authority, opportunity costs, and remaining constraints explicit.
mechanisms: Build credible assurance about the same joint plan; protection against failure would instead change payoffs.
Technical hunting risk is set aside. Promises alone may fail; the qualitative rankings do not establish risk dominance.

example_structure.scenario: Original stag/hare story now leads; Asha and Ben are stylized hunters in the principal illustration. One-shot simultaneous known-preference benchmark, no binding commitment or reputation, technical hunt risk set aside. Joint stag best, hare dependable, lone stag worst; both matching outcomes are equilibria. Acknowledged readiness may select the joint outcome; tutors’ limited guarantee remains a clearly separate modern application changing payoffs. Qualitative rankings do not establish risk dominance.
example_structure.changed_relationship: Build credible assurance about the same joint plan; protection against failure would instead change payoffs.
example_structure.residual_constraints: Technical hunting risk is set aside. Promises alone may fail; the qualitative rankings do not establish risk dominance.
example_structure.comparison: Qualitative choices, dependencies, and consequences; no invented scores, computed trajectory, or measured improvement claimed.

visual.question: Which choice is best when the other hunter joins?
visual.alternative_text: Hypothetical qualitative illustration. Asha and Ben choose stag or hare without observing the other’s choice. Both stag and both hare are double-outlined equilibria. Each prefers stag against stag, but hare against hare. A lone stag hunter loses the dependable fallback. Change: Build credible assurance about the same joint plan; protection against failure would instead change payoffs. Limitation: Technical hunting risk is set aside. Promises alone may fail; the qualitative rankings do not establish risk dominance.
visual.caption: Hypothetical illustration. Compare each hunter’s alternatives while holding the other’s action fixed. Mutual stag is preferred by both, yet mutual hare is also stable. Credible readiness and an acknowledged plan can support cooperation; they do not guarantee a partner or remove the cautious equilibrium.
